'''Mary Ellen Rudin''' (December 7, 1924 – March 18, 2013)<ref>{{cite news |title=In the Matter of the Estate of Mary Ellen Rudin |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/50040386/mary-ellen-rudin-1924-2013/ |newspaper=Wisconsin State Journal |date=May 11, 2013 |page=20 |via = [[Newspapers.com]] |accessdate=May 2, 2020}} {{Open access}}</ref> was an American [[mathematician]] known for her work in [[set-theoretic]] [[topology]].<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.journals.elsevier.com/topology-and-its-applications/news/mary-ellen-rudin-december-7-1924-march-18-2013/|title=Mary Ellen Rudin (December 7, 1924 – March 18, 2013)|publisher=webpage of [[Topology and its Applications]] published by [[Elsevier]]|accessdate=8 April 2013}}</ref> In 2013, [[Elsevier]] established the [[Mary Ellen Rudin Young Researcher Award]], which is awarded annually to a young researcher, mainly in fields adjacent to [[general topology]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Mary Ellen Rudin Young Researcher Award Fund |url=http://www.elsevier.com/awards/mary-ellen-rudin-young-researcher-award-fund |publisher=Elsevier |accessdate=23 March 2020}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==

Mary Ellen (Estill) Rudin was born in [[Hillsboro, Texas]] to Joe Jefferson Estill and Irene (Shook) Estill. Her mother Irene was an English teacher before marriage, and her father Joe was a civil engineer.  The family moved with her father's work, but spent a great deal of Mary Ellen's childhood around [[Leakey, Texas]].<ref name = "interview">Albers, D.J. and Reid, C. (1988) "An Interview with Mary Ellen Rudin". ''The College of Mathematics Journal'' 19(2) pp.114-137</ref> She had one sibling, a younger brother.  Both of Rudin's maternal grandmothers had attended [[Mary Sharp College]] near their hometown of [[Winchester, Tennessee]].  Rudin remarks on this legacy and how much her family valued education in an interview.<ref name= "interview" />

She attended the [[University of Texas at Austin|University of Texas]], completing her B.A. in 1944 after just three years before moving into the graduate program in mathematics under [[Robert Lee Moore]].<ref>{{MathGenealogy |id=308}}</ref> Her graduate thesis presented a counterexample to one of "Moore's axioms". She completed her Ph.D. in 1949.

During her time as an undergraduate, she was a member of the [[Phi Mu]] Women's Fraternity,<ref name="Phi Mu">{{cite book|title=Cactus Yearbook|year=1944|publisher=University of Texas|location=Austin, TX|page=394|url=http://mediasvc.ancestrylibrary.com/image/5b19bc58b519aa1a1e6a8459c726af42/128677668.jpg?MaxWidth=4500&MaxHeight=4500&Enhancement=AdaptiveContrast&ImageQuality=UltraHighQuality&client=SUI&version=cJ_HXtIBzwg|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230326033612/http://mediasvc.ancestrylibrary.com/image/5b19bc58b519aa1a1e6a8459c726af42/128677668.jpg?MaxWidth=4500&MaxHeight=4500&Enhancement=AdaptiveContrast&ImageQuality=UltraHighQuality&client=SUI&version=cJ_HXtIBzwg|url-status=dead|archive-date=March 26, 2023}}</ref>   and was elected to the [[Phi Beta Kappa]] society.<ref>{{cite book|title=Cactus Yearbook|year=1945|publisher=University of Texas|location=Austin, TX|page=141|url=http://mediasvc.ancestrylibrary.com/image/ac3541c932af215e09ea1af498ca461b/413209969.jpg?MaxWidth=4500&MaxHeight=4500&Enhancement=AdaptiveContrast&ImageQuality=UltraHighQuality&client=SUI&version=sPf5lNlJzwg}}{{dead link|date=January 2018 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

In 1953, she married mathematician [[Walter Rudin]], whom she met while teaching at [[Duke University]]. They had four children.

== Career ==
At the beginning of her career, Rudin taught at Duke University and the [[University of Rochester]].<ref name="AWM">"Mary Ellen Rudin", Profiles of Women in Mathematics. Association of Women in Mathematics [http://www.awm-math.org/noetherbrochure/Rudin84.html]. Accessed March 13, 2015.</ref> She took a position as lecturer at the [[University of Wisconsin at Madison|University of Wisconsin]] in 1959, and was appointed Professor of Mathematics in 1971.  After her retirement in 1991, she continued to serve as a Professor Emerita. She was the first [[Grace Chisholm Young]] Professor of Mathematics and also held the Hilidale Professorship.<ref name= "interview" /><ref name="AWM" />

She was an Invited Speaker of the [[International Congress of Mathematicians]] in 1974 in Vancouver.<ref>Rudin, Mary Ellen. [http://www.mathunion.org/ICM/ICM1974.2/Main/icm1974.2.0081.0086.ocr.pdf "The Normality of Products."] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171207020051/http://www.mathunion.org/ICM/ICM1974.2/Main/icm1974.2.0081.0086.ocr.pdf |date=2017-12-07 }} In ''Proceedings of the International Congress of Mathematicians, Vancouver, 1974'', vol. 1, pp. 81–86.</ref> She served as vice-president of the [[American Mathematical Society]], 1980–1981.  In 1984 she was selected to be a [[Noether Lecturer]]. She was an honorary member of the [[Hungarian Academy of Sciences]] (1995). In 2012 she became a fellow of the [[American Mathematical Society]].<ref>[https://www.ams.org/profession/fellows-list List of Fellows of the American Mathematical Society], retrieved 2013-07-07.</ref>

Rudin is best known in [[topology]] for her constructions of counterexamples to well-known conjectures.  In 1958, she found an [[Shelling (topology)|unshellable]] [[Triangulation (geometry)|triangulation]] of the [[tetrahedron]].<ref>{{Cite journal| volume = 64| issue = 3| pages = 90–91| last = Rudin| first = Mary Ellen| title = An unshellable triangulation of a tetrahedron
| journal = [[Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society]]| date = 1958-02-14| mr=0097055| doi=10.1090/s0002-9904-1958-10168-8| doi-access = free}}</ref> Most famously, Rudin was the first to construct a [[Dowker space]],<ref>{{cite journal |last=Rudin |first=Mary Ellen |author-link=Mary Ellen Rudin |date=1971 |title=A normal space ''X'' for which ''X × I'' is not normal |journal=[[Fundamenta Mathematicae|Fundam. Math.]] |volume=73 |number=2 |pages=179–186 |doi=10.4064/fm-73-2-179-186 |zbl=0224.54019 |doi-access=free }}</ref> which she did in 1971, thus disproving a conjecture of [[Clifford Hugh Dowker]] that had stood, and helped drive topological research, for more than twenty years. Her example fueled the search for "small" [[ZFC]] Dowker spaces. She, Keiko Chiba, and C. Przymusiński also proved the first [[Morita conjectures|Morita conjecture]] and a restricted version of the second.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Chiba|first1=Keiko|last2=Przymusinski|first2=Teodor C.|last3=Rudin|first3=Mary Ellen|author3-link=Mary Ellen Rudin|year=1986|title=Normality of product spaces and Morita's conjectures|journal=[[Topology and Its Applications]]|volume=22|issue=1|pages=19–32|doi=10.1016/0166-8641(86)90074-X|mr=0831178|doi-access=}}</ref> Her last major result was a proof of [[Nikiel's conjecture]].<ref>{{cite journal|first= Mary Ellen|last=Rudin|title=Nikiel's conjecture|journal= [[Topology and Its Applications]] |volume=116|year=2001|issue=3|pages=305–331|mr=1857669|doi=10.1016/S0166-8641(01)00218-8|doi-access=free}}</ref> Early proofs that every [[metric space]] is [[paracompact]] were somewhat involved, but Rudin provided an elementary one.<ref>{{cite journal|first= Mary Ellen|last=Rudin|url=https://www.ams.org/journals/proc/1969-020-02/S0002-9939-1969-0236876-3/S0002-9939-1969-0236876-3.pdf|title= A new proof that metric spaces are paracompact|journal= [[Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society]]|volume=20|issue= 2|year= 1969|page= 603|mr=0236876|doi=10.2307/2035708|jstor=2035708|doi-access=free}}</ref>

"Reading the articles of Mary Ellen Rudin, studying them until there is no mystery takes hours and hours; but those hours are rewarded, the student obtains power to which few have access. They are not hard to read, they are just hard mathematics, that's all." (Steve Watson<ref>W. S. Watson: Mary Ellen Rudin's early work on Suslin spaces, in: ''The work of Mary Ellen Rudin'', (Madison, WI, 1991), 168–182, Ann. New York Acad. Sci., '''705''', New York Acad. Sci., New York, 1993;</ref>)

== Later life ==
Rudin resided in [[Madison, Wisconsin]], in the [[Walter Rudin House|Rudin House]], a home designed by architect [[Frank Lloyd Wright]]. She died aged 88 on March 18, 2013.

== Mary Ellen Rudin Young Researcher Award ==
The '''Mary Ellen Rudin Young Researcher Award''' is an annual award given to young researchers in [[general topology]] and its related fields.<ref name="Mary Ellen Rudin Young Researcher Award">{{cite web | title=Mary Ellen Rudin Young Researcher Award | website=ScienceDirect.com by Elsevier | date=2023-11-07 | url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/journal/topology-and-its-applications/about/awards#introduction-to-mary-ellen-rudin | access-date=2024-01-03}}</ref> It was established in 2013 by [[Elsevier]] on behalf of the journal ''[[Topology and its Applications]]'' and consists of US$15,000 that must be used by the awardee in the following way: US$5,000 for three major conferences in topology, US$5,000 for visiting a research center, and US$5,000, which can be used freely and is regarded as a cash prize.

The prize was named after Rudin. Rudin gave her permission to use her name for the award but died before the first prize was awarded.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Memories of Mary Ellen Rudin |journal=Notices of the American Mathematical Society |date=June–July 2015 |volume=62 |issue=6 |page=619 |url=https://www.ams.org/notices/201506/201506-full-issue.pdf |accessdate=24 March 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Benkart |first1=Georgia |title=A Tribute to Mary Ellen Rudin |url=https://celebratio.org/Rudin_Mary/article/544/ |website=[[Celebratio Mathematica]] |publisher=Mathematical Science Publishers |accessdate=24 March 2020}}</ref>
